 From FAA to TSA: Al Klukowski 
 Thursday, November 19, 2026 
 On the morning of Sept. 10, 2001, Washington state-based Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) Civil Aviation Security Inspector Albert Klukowski accepted an FAA international security position in Frankfurt, Germany. By the close of the following day, those plans were on hold.  
  Within 17 hours of the first terrorist plane strike in New York on what became known as 9/11, Klukowski had thrown a hastily packed bag into a government vehicle and had driven five hours along deserted highways to Spokane International Airport. Once there, he checked in with airport police and, fatigued from the day’s events, sought a few hours of sleep. His FAA colleagues found themselves in similar situations. 
  “One thing that really stuck with me was walking out onto the tarmac and hearing nothing but the wind,” Klukowski said of the unprecedented national ground stop. “It was the eeriest feeling I’ve ever had in my life: no tugs, no people, no planes moving.” 
  By the time he was able to assume his Frankfurt role six months later, the federal agency of record on Klukowski’s business cards read U.S. Department of Transportation (DOT) – Transportation Security Administration (TSA). By August, another transfer, this time from DOT to DHS, was noted on his Notification of Personnel Action, or Standard Form-50, an official federal employment record. 
  “It’s the only time I’ve ever seen an SF-50 read ‘mass transfer’,” Klukowski said of the sweeping personnel action. 
  Klukowski is quick to point out that through all the organizational changes, the security mission didn’t change, and the dedication of aviation security professionals never wavered.  
  In observance of TSA’s 25th anniversary, Klukowski, currently serving as a Transportation Security Specialist at the Dallas Regional Operations Center, reflected on TSA’s present and future mission through the lens of its history. By describing the aviation security landscape pre-9/11 and the changes Congress mandated afterward, he explained how FAA employees became some of TSA’s first professionals. 
  “I began my aviation security career in early 1997,” Klukowski said, “so my experience in aviation security predated TSA. I think it’s important to understand the past, because unfortunately, everything we’ve done and everything we continue to do is because there have been victims of a horrible tragedy.” 
  Klukowski remembers that prior to the Aviation and Transportation Security Act , which established TSA, the FAA’s Civil Aviation Security Division (CASD), headquartered in Washington D.C., managed all civil aviation security functions. At that time, the CASD organizational chart included seven regional and multiple field offices and units (CASFOs/CASFUs); international field offices in Brussels, Frankfurt and Singapore; and the technical center and Federal Air Marshal (FAM) facility in Atlantic City, New Jersey.   
  “The primary function of the CASFOs/CASFUs was very similar to what the Assistant Federal Security Director for Inspections and Transportation Security Inspectors do now,” Klukowski said, “ensuring that airports, airlines and other regulated entities follow the regulations and security programs. They identified vulnerabilities, and if necessary, opened investigations for noncompliance.”   
   The international team assessed foreign airports with flights to the United States to verify compliance with international security standards and inspected all U.S.-bound flights. Atlantic City served as a hub for research and development of emerging screening technologies and the home base for the Federal Air Marshal Service. 
  “All these people found themselves working with their industry partners starting the morning of September 12, 2001, trying to piece together a shattered civil aviation system,” Klukowski said. “For the first week, many of us found ourselves sitting in conference rooms with airport security coordinators, airline station managers, law enforcement and others, reviewing security directives and emergency amendments issued by headquarters, identifying potential implementation issues, and providing feedback for revisions. Some, who previously served as FAMs found themselves once again holstering a sidearm and rejoining the ranks.   
  “Domestically, during the first month, Civil Aviation Security Inspectors were posted daily at all the Category X, I and even some Category II airport screening checkpoints. Some FAA personnel also trained U.S. Army and Air National Guard units deployed nationwide. The full-time Federal Air Marshals unit, as well as those previously trained as FAMs, began onboarding and training hundreds more. Internationally, inspectors were sent to dozens of foreign locations to confirm that new security procedures for flights to the U.S. were being implemented.”   
  As our nation’s transitioned aviation security into TSA’s new organizational structure, former FAA aviation personnel became some of TSA’s first employees. Many went on to build long careers with TSA, acquiring unparalleled institutional knowledge fundamental to our current success. 
  TSA has continued its mission of protecting the aviation system, not just in the U.S., but internationally as well.  When asked about his future, Klukowski said his hope is to remain in TSA’s international operations.   
  “Working with countries and airports around the globe that have far less funding, infrastructure, and resources than TSA, and helping them improve their aviation security (AVSEC) systems, is what drives me every day,” Klukowski said. “I have worked with AVSEC officials at 80 foreign airports in 38 countries. Knowing I have helped improve their AVSEC systems as part of a team is something I want to continue doing for as long as I can.” 
  By Karen Robicheaux, Strategic Communications and Public Affairs
